name: General Data Protection Regulation
evidence_rating: strong: several peer-reviewed causal studies (mostly short-run, digital sector); Commission reviews give enforcement statistics but no cost-benefit estimate
summary: Independent causal studies consistently find costs: less venture funding, fewer apps (a third exited, entry halved), higher data costs (+22%), lower recorded web traffic (-12%) and more concentration among web vendors favouring Google and Facebook. The Commission's reviews report rising enforcement (EUR 4.2bn in fines) and better-resourced regulators, but the promised EUR 2.3bn a year in administrative savings has never been evaluated.

indicators.objective: Ensure consistent enforcement of data protection rules
Rationalise the governance system to help ensure more consistent enforcement

indicators.indicator: Time and costs spent by data controllers in complying with legislation in other Member States
indicators.evidence: Not measured. Commission reports describe fragmentation in national implementation and inconsistent interpretation, but give no cost or time series.

indicators.indicator: Resources allocated to data protection authorities
indicators.evidence: Measured: between 2020 and 2024 all but two authorities gained staff; increase above 25% in 14 Member States (Ireland +79%). Authorities still cite insufficient resources as the main limit on enforcement.

indicators.indicator: Established data protection officers in public and private organisations
Use made of data protection impact assessments
indicators.evidence: No systematic data; report notes SMEs need templates and guidance for DPIAs.

indicators.indicator: Number of complaints by data subjects and compensation received
indicators.evidence: Complaint handling and amicable settlements described; cross-border cooperation ~2,400 case entries; compensation not quantified.

indicators.indicator: Number of cases leading to prosecution of data controllers
indicators.evidence: Not reported as such; corrective measures vary widely between authorities.

indicators.indicator: Fines imposed on controllers responsible for breaches
indicators.evidence: Measured: over 6,680 fines totalling about EUR 4.2bn (Ireland EUR 2.8bn, Luxembourg EUR 746m). Nine binding EDPB dispute-resolution decisions.

indicators.indicator: Net administrative-burden saving of about EUR 2.3bn per year (baseline fragmentation cost about EUR 2.9bn/yr)
indicators.evidence: Never evaluated. Independent studies instead find substantial compliance and data costs (data costs +22%, tech-firm profits -2.1%).
indicators.status: not measured (independent evidence points the other way)
indicators.sources: SEC(2012) 72/73; Demirer et al.; Frey & Presidente

literature.citation: European Commission (2012), Impact Assessment accompanying the data protection reform (executive summary SEC(2012) 73), SEC(2012) 72
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the data protection reform (executive summary SEC(2012) 73)
literature.method: ex-ante (Standard Cost Model)
literature.headline: Fragmentation costs firms about EUR 2.9bn/yr in administrative burden; the reform would save about EUR 2.3bn/yr
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected the GDPR to cut red tape for businesses by about EUR 2.3 billion a year by replacing 28 national regimes with one.
literature.quality: forecast; covers administrative burden only, not compliance costs

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Second report on the application of the General Data Protection Regulation, COM(2024) 357
literature.title: Second report on the application of the General Data Protection Regulation
literature.method: review (enforcement statistics, stakeholder input)
literature.headline: Over 6,680 fines (~EUR 4.2bn); DPA staff up >25% in 14 Member States; calls for more support for SMEs and more consistent interpretation; no estimate of costs or benefits
literature.summary_plain: The Commission judges the GDPR to be working but says enforcement is uneven between countries and SMEs need more practical help.
literature.quality: self-evaluation; no economic impact estimates

literature.citation: Jia, Jin & Wagman (2021), The Short-Run Effects of the General Data Protection Regulation on Technology Venture Investment, Marketing Science (NBER w25248)
literature.title: The Short-Run Effects of the General Data Protection Regulation on Technology Venture Investment
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences (EU vs US ventures)
literature.headline: Negative post-GDPR effects on EU tech ventures relative to US ones in the number of deals, total amounts raised and amount per deal
literature.summary_plain: After the GDPR, EU technology start-ups raised less venture funding, in fewer deals, than comparable US start-ups.
literature.quality: short-run only

literature.citation: Johnson, Shriver & Goldberg (2023), Privacy and Market Concentration: Intended and Unintended Consequences of the GDPR, Management Science 69(10)
literature.title: Privacy and Market Concentration: Intended and Unintended Consequences of the GDPR
literature.method: causal: event study (27,000+ websites)
literature.headline: Website use of web-technology vendors fell 15% for EU users in the week after enforcement; vendor-market concentration rose 17%, mainly benefiting Google and Facebook; aggregate effects faded by end-2018 but persisted for advertising vendors
literature.summary_plain: The GDPR led websites to drop smaller data vendors, increasing the market share of Google and Facebook.
literature.quality: short-run; persistence only for ad vendors

literature.citation: Goldberg, Johnson & Shriver (2024), Regulating Privacy Online: An Economic Evaluation of the GDPR, American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 16(1)
literature.title: Regulating Privacy Online: An Economic Evaluation of the GDPR
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences (1,084 online firms, Adobe Analytics)
literature.headline: About 12% fewer recorded EU page views and 12% less recorded website revenue after enforcement, decomposed into real effects and reduced data recording
literature.summary_plain: Websites recorded about 12% fewer visits and revenue from EU users after the GDPR, partly because less data was collected.
literature.quality: measured effect mixes real and recording effects

literature.citation: Peukert, Bechtold, Batikas & Kretschmer (2022), Regulatory Spillovers and Data Governance: Evidence from the GDPR, Marketing Science
literature.title: Regulatory Spillovers and Data Governance: Evidence from the GDPR
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences (websites)
literature.headline: The GDPR affected websites beyond the EU and increased market concentration among web technology vendors
literature.summary_plain: The GDPR's effects spread beyond the EU and strengthened the position of the largest web-technology providers.

literature.citation: Janssen, Kesler, Kummer & Waldfogel (2022), GDPR and the Lost Generation of Innovative Apps, NBER Working Paper 30028
literature.title: GDPR and the Lost Generation of Innovative Apps
literature.method: causal + structural model (4.1m Google Play apps, 2016-2019)
literature.headline: GDPR induced the exit of about a third of available apps; new app entry fell by half; long-run consumer surplus and app usage about a third lower
literature.summary_plain: The GDPR pushed about a third of apps off Google Play and halved the launch of new apps, reducing consumer welfare by an estimated third.
literature.quality: structural model drives the welfare estimate

literature.citation: Frey & Presidente (2024), Privacy regulation and firm performance: Estimating the GDPR effect globally, Economic Inquiry
literature.title: Privacy regulation and firm performance: Estimating the GDPR effect globally
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences by exposure to EU markets
literature.headline: Technology firms targeting EU consumers saw profits fall 2.1% (no effect on sales); higher extra expenses and wage bills; faster patenting in GDPR-related technologies
literature.summary_plain: Firms exposed to the EU market earned slightly lower profits after the GDPR because of higher compliance costs, though they also patented more in privacy technology.

literature.citation: Demirer, Jimenez-Hernandez, Li & Peng (2024), Data, Privacy Laws and Firm Production: Evidence from the GDPR, NBER Working Paper 32146 (rev. Feb 2026)
literature.title: Data, Privacy Laws and Firm Production: Evidence from the GDPR
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences (cloud-computing provider data) + production function
literature.headline: EU firms cut data storage 26% and data processing 15% vs US firms; equivalent to a 22% rise in the cost of data, but only 0.1-0.6% higher overall production costs
literature.summary_plain: The GDPR made data about 22% more expensive for EU firms, so they stored and processed less, though the effect on total costs was small.

literature.citation: Aridor, Che & Salz (2023), The Effect of Privacy Regulation on the Data Industry: Empirical Evidence from GDPR, RAND Journal of Economics (NBER w26900)
literature.title: The Effect of Privacy Regulation on the Data Industry: Empirical Evidence from GDPR
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences (online travel intermediary)
literature.headline: Opt-in requirement cut observed consumers by 12.5%, but remaining consumers were tracked longer and became more valuable to advertisers, offsetting part of the loss
literature.summary_plain: About 1 in 8 users opted out of tracking under the GDPR; those who stayed became easier to track and more valuable to advertisers.
literature.quality: single firm

literature.citation: Diegmann & Kubis (2025), Die Betriebe mussten in den letzten drei Jahren 325.000 Arbeitskräfte zusätzlich einstellen, um die gewachsene Bürokratie zu bewältigen, IAB-Forum (Institute for Employment Research, Germany), 20 October 2025
literature.title: Die Betriebe mussten in den letzten drei Jahren 325.000 Arbeitskräfte zusätzlich einstellen, um die gewachsene Bürokratie zu bewältigen
literature.venue: IAB-Forum (Institute for Employment Research, Germany), 20 October 2025
literature.method: firm survey: IAB Job Vacancy Survey Q1 2025, 9,209 establishments; self-reported, retrospective over three years
literature.outcomes: compliance costs; employment; productivity; investment; innovation
literature.headline: 68% of German establishments name the GDPR as the regulation that burdens them most (next: EU IT-security rules 32%, supply-chain due diligence act 14%). Across all bureaucracy, 11% of establishments hired extra staff to cope, about 325,000 workers in three years; 80% report higher costs, 55% productivity losses, 19% investment and 16% innovation obstacles.
literature.summary_plain: A large survey of German firms finds the GDPR is the rule they find most burdensome; rising red tape overall led them to hire about 325,000 extra staff in three years and, by their own account, cost productivity.
literature.quality: self-reported survey; covers all bureaucracy, not the GDPR alone; no counterfactual

literature.authors: Klaus M. Miller, Karlo Lukic, Bernd Skiera
literature.title: The Impact of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) on Online Tracking
literature.venue: arXiv:2411.06862 (econ.GN); earlier NBER conference/working paper versions
literature.method: difference-in-differences on balanced panel of 294 publishers (WhoTracks.me data, May 2017-Dec 2019), EU publishers vs unaffected control
literature.outcomes: number and type of third-party trackers per website
literature.headline: GDPR reduced about four trackers per publisher, a 14.79% decrease relative to the control group, mainly privacy-invasive trackers; little effect on advertising trackers.
literature.summary_plain: Websites covered by the GDPR added fewer tracking tools than comparable websites outside its reach, especially the trackers that collect and share personal data.
literature.quality: Credible DiD with control group; modest sample of 294 publishers; tracker counts from one data provider
literature.citation: Klaus M. Miller, Karlo Lukic, Bernd Skiera (2024), The Impact of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) on Online Tracking, arXiv:2411.06862 (econ.GN); earlier NBER conference/working paper versions

literature.authors: Klaus M. Miller, Bernd Skiera, Julia Schmitt
literature.title: The Impact of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) on Online Usage Behavior
literature.method: generalized synthetic control on visits to 6,387 websites in 24 industries and 13 countries, 11 months before and 19 months after enforcement
literature.outcomes: website visits, unique visitors, visits per visitor
literature.headline: Weekly visits fell by 4.88% within 3 months and 10.02% after 18 months, driven by fewer unique visitors (-6.61%); about a quarter of websites gained.
literature.summary_plain: After the GDPR, websites affected by it got about 10% fewer visits after a year and a half, mostly because fewer people visited, although some sites gained users at others' expense.
literature.period_geography: 2017-2019; 13 countries, EU users/EU websites vs others
literature.quality: Strong causal design on very large data; traffic data from a single analytics provider
literature.citation: Klaus M. Miller, Bernd Skiera, Julia Schmitt (2024), The Impact of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) on Online Usage Behavior, arXiv:2411.11589 (v2 2026)

literature.authors: Raffaele Congiu, Lorien Sabatino, Geza Sapi
literature.title: The Impact of Privacy Regulation on Web Traffic: Evidence From the GDPR
literature.method: difference-in-differences on traffic data for ~5,000 web domains in Europe and the US
literature.headline: GDPR reduced website traffic by about 15% in the long run, with smallest and largest sites losing most and effects amplified after the first major fine.
literature.summary_plain: European websites lost roughly 15% of their visitors after the GDPR compared with US sites, and the drop grew after regulators began fining firms.
literature.quality: DiD with US control; traffic estimates from third-party panel (SimilarWeb-type) data
literature.citation: Raffaele Congiu, Lorien Sabatino, Geza Sapi (2022), The Impact of Privacy Regulation on Web Traffic: Evidence From the GDPR, Information Economics and Policy 61, 101003

literature.authors: Miguel Godinho de Matos, Idris Adjerid
literature.title: Consumer Consent and Firm Targeting After GDPR: The Case of a Large Telecom Provider
literature.method: field experiment around GDPR-compliant consent elicitation at a large European telecom provider
literature.outcomes: consumer opt-in rates, sales, marketing efficacy, contractual lock-in
literature.headline: Opt-in for data uses rose once GDPR-compliant consent was elicited, and sales, marketing efficacy and contractual lock-in increased, while consumers kept restricting sensitive uses.
literature.summary_plain: When a telecom firm asked customers for consent the GDPR way, more customers agreed to share data, and the firm then sold more through better-targeted marketing.
literature.quality: Experimental variation within a single firm; external validity limited
literature.citation: Miguel Godinho de Matos, Idris Adjerid (2022), Consumer Consent and Firm Targeting After GDPR: The Case of a Large Telecom Provider, Management Science 68(5): 3330-3378

literature.authors: Knut Blind, Crispin Niebel, Christian Rammer
literature.title: The impact of the EU General data protection regulation on product innovation
literature.method: conditional difference-in-differences with firm fixed effects on German innovation survey (Mannheim Innovation Panel)
literature.headline: GDPR led to a substantial shift from radical to incremental product innovation in German firms.
literature.summary_plain: German firms affected by the GDPR did more improving of existing products and less developing of entirely new ones, as compliance absorbed resources.
literature.quality: DiD on representative firm survey panel; treatment intensity self-reported
literature.citation: Knut Blind, Crispin Niebel, Christian Rammer (2024), The impact of the EU General data protection regulation on product innovation, Industry and Innovation 31(3): 311-351 (earlier ZEW DP 22-047)

literature.authors: Vincent Lefrere, Logan Warberg, Cristobal Cheyre, Veronica Marotta, Alessandro Acquisti
literature.title: Does Privacy Regulation Harm Content Providers? A Longitudinal Analysis of the Impact of the GDPR
literature.method: difference-in-differences on longitudinal panel of EU and US news and media websites
literature.outcomes: tracking, consent mechanisms, content production, quality proxies, traffic, survival, monetization
literature.headline: EU news sites cut tracking more than US sites and saw fewer page views per user, but no negative effect on new content provision, content quality, survival or monetization.
literature.summary_plain: European news websites collected less data after the GDPR but kept producing as much content of similar quality as US sites, and did not close more often.
literature.quality: DiD with US control and many outcomes; sample limited to news/media sites
literature.citation: Vincent Lefrere, Logan Warberg, Cristobal Cheyre, Veronica Marotta, Alessandro Acquisti (2024), Does Privacy Regulation Harm Content Providers? A Longitudinal Analysis of the Impact of the GDPR, Management Science (forthcoming/published; HAL hal-05222559)

literature.title: Short-term Impacts of the GDPR on Firm Performance
literature.method: difference-in-differences on firm-level financial panel of European and US companies 2014-2018
literature.headline: Profit margins of EU data-intensive firms rose about 1.7-3.4 percentage points less than US counterparts in the first GDPR year; SMEs hit hardest, no difference for very large firms.
literature.summary_plain: In the GDPR's first year, European companies that rely heavily on data saw their profit margins grow less than similar US companies, with smaller firms affected most.
literature.quality: DiD with US control; only one post-period year; data-intensity classification by industry
literature.citation: Heli Koski, Nelli Valmari (2020), Short-term Impacts of the GDPR on Firm Performance, ETLA Working Papers No. 77

literature.authors: James Bessen, Stephen Michael Impink, Lydia Reichensperger, Robert Seamans
literature.title: GDPR and the Importance of Data to AI Startups
literature.venue: SSRN working paper / BU Technology & Policy Research Initiative
literature.method: survey of AI startups in more than 25 countries with regression analysis
literature.outcomes: data deletion, resource reallocation, new GDPR positions
literature.headline: Nearly three quarters of surveyed AI startups reported deleting some data because of GDPR; firms with European customers were more likely to create GDPR positions or reallocate resources.
literature.summary_plain: Most AI start-ups surveyed said they had deleted data to comply with the GDPR, and those selling in Europe more often had to shift staff and money to compliance.
literature.quality: Self-reported survey, no counterfactual; moderate sample
literature.citation: James Bessen, Stephen Michael Impink, Lydia Reichensperger, Robert Seamans (2020), GDPR and the Importance of Data to AI Startups, SSRN working paper / BU Technology & Policy Research Initiative

literature.authors: Martin Degeling, Christine Utz, Christopher Lentzsch, Henry Hosseini, Florian Schaub, Thorsten Holz
literature.title: We Value Your Privacy ... Now Take Some Cookies: Measuring the GDPR's Impact on Web Privacy
literature.method: longitudinal web measurement of the 500 most popular websites in each of 28 EU states (6,579 sites)
literature.headline: By May 2018, 84.5% of websites had privacy policies (72.6% of existing ones updated) and 62.1% displayed cookie consent notices, 16% more than in January 2018.
literature.summary_plain: Around the GDPR start date, most popular European websites updated their privacy policies and many more began showing cookie banners.
literature.quality: Large before/after crawl; no control group; measures form rather than substance of compliance
literature.citation: Martin Degeling, Christine Utz, Christopher Lentzsch, Henry Hosseini, Florian Schaub, Thorsten Holz (2019), We Value Your Privacy ... Now Take Some Cookies: Measuring the GDPR's Impact on Web Privacy, NDSS Symposium 2019

literature.authors: Midas Nouwens, Ilaria Liccardi, Michael Veale, David Karger, Lalana Kagal
literature.title: Dark Patterns after the GDPR: Scraping Consent Pop-ups and Demonstrating their Influence
literature.method: web scrape of consent pop-ups of five main CMPs on UK top-10,000 sites (n=680) plus field experiment with 40 participants
literature.outcomes: compliance of consent designs, consent rates
literature.headline: Only 11.8% of consent pop-ups met minimal requirements based on EU law; removing the first-page opt-out raised consent by 22-23 percentage points.
literature.summary_plain: Almost nine in ten cookie consent pop-ups on major UK websites did not meet basic legal requirements, and design tricks clearly pushed people into agreeing.
literature.quality: Compliance measurement with clear criteria; small experiment; UK only
literature.citation: Midas Nouwens, Ilaria Liccardi, Michael Veale, David Karger, Lalana Kagal (2020), Dark Patterns after the GDPR: Scraping Consent Pop-ups and Demonstrating their Influence, CHI 2020 (ACM)

literature.authors: Bernhard Ganglmair, Julia Krämer, Jacopo Gambato
literature.title: Regulatory Compliance With Limited Enforceability: Evidence From Privacy Policies
literature.venue: ZEW Discussion Paper No. 24-012 / CRC TR 224 DP 547
literature.method: text-as-data analysis of a large panel of German firms' privacy policies before and after GDPR, with inspection model
literature.outcomes: disclosure volume and readability of privacy policies
literature.headline: Firms increased disclosure volume in privacy policies after GDPR but readability did not improve; better-funded data protection authorities induced better readability.
literature.summary_plain: German companies wrote longer privacy policies after the GDPR, but they did not get any easier to read, except where regulators had more money to enforce.
literature.quality: Large text panel; before/after with heterogeneity, no clean control group
literature.citation: Bernhard Ganglmair, Julia Krämer, Jacopo Gambato (2024), Regulatory Compliance With Limited Enforceability: Evidence From Privacy Policies, ZEW Discussion Paper No. 24-012 / CRC TR 224 DP 547

literature.title: Special Eurobarometer 487a: The General Data Protection Regulation
literature.method: representative survey of about 27,000 Europeans (March 2019)
literature.outcomes: awareness of GDPR, data rights and data protection authorities
literature.headline: 73% had heard of at least one of six GDPR rights, 67% knew about the GDPR and 57% about their national data protection authority; 62% worried about lacking control of data online.
literature.summary_plain: A year after the GDPR, two-thirds of Europeans had heard of it and most knew at least one of their new rights, but many still felt they lacked control over their data.
literature.quality: Large representative survey; awareness only, no pre-GDPR baseline in same form
literature.interested_party: European Commission (commissioned by the act's author)
literature.citation: European Commission (Kantar) (2019), Special Eurobarometer 487a: The General Data Protection Regulation, European Commission, June 2019
